<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, you are dealing with a Node.js–based CLI tool called “Task Master” for AI-driven development using Claude (and optionally Perplexity) that integrates closely with Cursor AI. The project’s single responsibility is to manage tasks—from parsing product requirement documents (PRDs) to generating, expanding, and tracking tasks (and subtasks) through various CLI commands. Here’s how you can draw the system design diagram for this project:

1. Main Components Identification:
   • CLI Interface & Command Module: Represent the CLI entrypoints (e.g., the scripts in the “bin” folder, “index.js”, and the commands available in “scripts/modules”). These modules include command handling for “init”, “parse-prd”, “list”, “next”, “generate”, “set-status”, “expand”, etc.
   • Core Task Management: This includes the logic for creating and tracking tasks defined in “tasks” and “tasks.json” along with the corresponding tool files in “mcp-server/src/tools” (like addTask, expandTask, etc.) that process task operations.
   • AI Integration and External APIs: Components for interfacing with Anthropic (Claude API) and optionally OpenAI/Perplexity. This layer handles configuration (using environment variables from .env) and processes responses from the APIs.
   • Cursor AI Integration: The “.cursor” directory (especially the “.cursor/rules” files) and integration instructions detailed in the README show how Cursor AI leverages pre-configured rules to understand the workflow. Also, the MCP server under “mcp-server” establishes a bridge using the Model Control Protocol.
   • Supporting and Utility Modules: Included in “scripts/modules” (such as dependency-manager, ui, commands, ai-services, etc.) and “tests” for unit and integration flows to verify functionality.
   • Configuration & Assets: Folders like “assets”, “.changeset”, and configuration files (package.json, .env.example, etc.) are used for configuration, changelog management, and deployment/documentation.

2. Relationship and Interaction Mapping:
   • The CLI component is the entry point that triggers various commands. It interacts directly with the core task management logic (found in “mcp-server/src/tools” and “scripts/modules”) to perform actions such as initializing projects, parsing PRDs, or generating task files.
   • The Core Task Management module interacts with persistent artifacts (tasks stored in “tasks” and aggregated in “tasks.json”) and with external API wrappers for AI-driven task generation.
   • AI Integration: When commands like “parse-prd” or “expand” are executed, the CLI layer calls the AI services through your modules (ai-services) which in turn use the Anthropic SDK (and optionally Perplexity) based on the configured environment controls.
   • Cursor AI integration uses its own set of rules (in “.cursor/rules”) to monitor and drive the workflow; additionally, it connects to the MCP server component to forward task commands from Cursor.
   • Testing and utilities are interconnected: the “tests” folder ensures all modules (from command logic to dependency management) perform as expected.

3. Architectural Patterns & Important Design Choices:
   • Modular Design: The system is broken into many independent modules (commands, task management, dependency management) to ensure separation of concerns.
   • CLI/Command-Based Architecture: Each command (e.g., “init”, “list”, “next”, “generate”, “expand”) is treated as a standalone operation that uses the common core.
   • External Service Integration: Clear abstraction layers exist for talking with the Anthropic API, Perplexity, and the integration with Cursor, which likely uses well-defined interfaces.
   • ES Modules: With native ES modules (as indicated in the README), the project uses modern JavaScript module conventions.
   • Test-Driven & Configurable: The presence of “tests” and configuration files shows an emphasis on ensuring reliability and customizability.

4. Relevant Technologies, Frameworks, and Libraries:
   • Node.js (v14+) and ES modules.
   • Anthropic SDK for Claude API integration.
   • Optionally OpenAI SDK (for Perplexity API).
   • npm for dependency, scripts, and package management.
   • Integration with Cursor AI (leveraging .cursor rules and MCP server patterns).

5. Guidelines for Diagram Tailoring (for a Full-Stack CLI & AI Workflow Tool):
   • Create separate sections for:
     - CLI/Entry Layer: Illustrate command triggers from “bin” scripts and “index.js”.
     - Core Functionality: Group task management operations along with submodules found inside “mcp-server/src/tools” and “scripts/modules”.
     - External Interfaces: Draw arrows for API calls to Anthropic (Claude API) and optional Perplexity, plus the interaction with Cursor AI through MCP.
     - Persistence & Configuration: Box representing configuration files, tasks (tasks.json and individual task files), and environmental variables.
     - Test and Utility Modules: Separate unit test components and utilities to support core functions.
   • Use directional arrows both to show incoming command flow from the user (via CLI) to the core modules and then outgoing API calls.
   • Distinguish different layers (CLI, Business Logic, Data/API, Integration) using color coding or shapes. For example:
     - Rectangles for modules (CLI, Task Manager, AI Services) 
     - Cylinders for external services (Anthropic API, Perplexity API)
     - Rounded rectangles or clouds for Cursor AI integration.
     - Document icons for configuration files and asset data.

6. Instructing the Principal Software Engineer:
   • Label each component clearly (e.g., “CLI Engine”, “Task Manager”, “API Integrator”, “Cursor AI Module”).
   • Draw directional arrows to indicate data flow: from user command to the CLI layer; then from the CLI to the task command modules; and from there to both persistent files (tasks JSON, individual task files) and external APIs.
   • Include color coding or shape variants to instantly signal the type of component (e.g., blue for external services, green for business logic, gray for configuration).
   • Emphasize the middleware nature of “mcp-server” and the encapsulated “scripts/modules” that act as service providers.
   • Lastly, highlight that these architectural elements resonate with the modular and plug-and-play design of the system—a key design philosophy behind AI-driven task management tools.

By mapping these components and interactions accurately in the diagram, you can provide a comprehensive overview of “Task Master” that illustrates how a CLI command triggers a chain of internal processes, interacts with external AI services, and communicates with Cursor AI to deliver an integrated task management workflow. This detailed and visually differentiated representation will be invaluable during design reviews and for onboarding developers onto the project.
</explanation>
